a_rows_sample.anchor: Known dimension, unknown value: P(expiry date|O). This is ordinary uncertainty about a known dimension. Unknown dimension: P(additional relevant dimension exists|O). This is uncertainty about the structure of the knowledge space. ... your point is primarily about the second one.
a_rows_sample.statement: Distinguishes two fundamentally different uncertainties: (1) known dimension, unknown value -- e.g. we know certificate expiry is relevant but not its date, P(expiry date|O), ordinary uncertainty about a known dimension; and (2) unknown dimension -- we don't know whether some additional dependency is relevant at all, P(additional relevant dimension exists|O), uncertainty about the structure of the knowledge space itself. Example: known dimensions (version, CPU, memory, repositories, network) may be well understood while other potential dimensions (identity integration, backup dependency, certificate dependency, licensing, external services, disaster recovery, operational dependency) remain undiscovered as even being relevant.

a_rows_sample.statement: Shows why more information does not automatically mean more knowledge: Person A knows 5 dimensions extremely precisely; Person B knows 20 dimensions reasonably well and may have more knowledge overall by having discovered more of the relevant state space despite less precision per dimension; Person C knows 5 dimensions extremely well AND knows that many dimensions may remain undiscovered -- Person C has lower completeness confidence but arguably better epistemic awareness than either A or B.

a_rows_sample.statement: Corrects the interpretation of a stated confidence like '95% knowledge': it likely means P(we have identified the relevant dimensions sufficiently) approx 0.95, not P(each fact is correct)=0.95 -- these are completely different quantities. Separates three distinct epistemic properties that a single percentage conflates: dimension coverage (e.g. 95%), information accuracy (e.g. 99%), and reasoning confidence (e.g. 90%).

a_rows_sample.statement: Formalizes D_t as the relevant dimensions of the ideal state at time t (not fully known), with hat-D_t subset D_t as the discovered subset, and observed information O_t(hat-D_t) about discovered dimensions; splits the problem into two: D_t -> hat-D_t (the dimension-discovery problem: which dimensions exist/are relevant) and I_t(hat-D_t) -> K_t (the state-extraction problem: what do we know about those dimensions).

a_rows_sample.anchor: KnowledgeOS cannot only store: "What do we know?" It must somehow preserve: "What dimensions of the subject do we currently believe are relevant?" and "How confident are we that our dimensional model is complete enough?" ... KnowledgeOS should potentially be able to say: "We have strong evidence concerning these dimensions, but there is unresolved uncertainty about whether additional relevant dimensions exist." That is a much more honest representation of knowledge.
a_rows_sample.statement: Argues KnowledgeOS cannot only store 'what do we know' -- it must also preserve which dimensions are currently believed relevant and how confident the system is that its dimensional model is complete enough; without this, an AI could falsely claim 'I know everything about Nexus' when it has only modeled a handful of dimensions well. KnowledgeOS should instead be able to honestly say it has strong evidence on known dimensions but unresolved uncertainty about whether additional relevant dimensions exist.

a_rows_sample.anchor: Uncertainty begins not only when we don't know the value of something. It begins earlier -- when we don't know what things or dimensions are relevant to know about. ... Knowledge completeness = dimension coverage + information completeness within those dimensions, with uncertainty potentially existing at both levels.
a_rows_sample.statement: States the key insight simply: uncertainty begins not only when we don't know the value of something, but earlier -- when we don't know what dimensions are relevant to know about at all; therefore Knowledge completeness = dimension coverage + information completeness within those dimensions, with uncertainty potentially existing at both levels.

a_rows_sample.anchor: whether "dimension" is the right primitive at all, or whether what you are describing is more fundamentally a space of possible questions/propositions about the ideal state. That distinction could be decisive for the eventual mathematical model.
a_rows_sample.statement: Raises an open question that could be decisive for the eventual mathematical model: whether 'dimension' is the right primitive at all for this analysis, or whether what is being described is more fundamentally a space of possible questions/propositions about the ideal state.

a_rows_sample.anchor: Few dimensions known / Many dimensions known x Little information per dimension / A lot of information per dimension -- Very low knowledge / Low-medium knowledge / Medium knowledge / High knowledge. But there is a crucial fifth question: How confident are we that we have discovered most of the relevant dimensions? So Knowledge may involve: Dimension Coverage x Information Quality x Determination Quality.
a_rows_sample.statement: Presents a 2x2 knowledge matrix crossing dimension count (few/many known) against information quality (little/a lot per dimension), yielding four qualitative knowledge levels (very low, low/medium, medium, high); adds a crucial fifth question -- confidence that most relevant dimensions have been discovered -- proposing conceptually (not yet as a formula) that Knowledge involves Dimension Coverage x Information Quality x Determination Quality.

a_rows_sample.anchor: Team A knows version, CPU, RAM with extremely accurate information. Team B knows version, CPU, RAM, network, dependencies, certificates, backup, authentication, monitoring, licensing, but some of their information is uncertain. It is entirely possible that: Knowledge(B) > Knowledge(A) ... Because Team B has broader dimension coverage.
a_rows_sample.statement: Worked example: Team A knows only version/CPU/RAM but with extremely accurate information; Team B knows ten dimensions (version, CPU, RAM, network, dependencies, certificates, backup, authentication, monitoring, licensing) but some information is uncertain; despite Team A's higher per-dimension accuracy, Knowledge(B) > Knowledge(A) is entirely possible because Team B has broader dimension coverage.

a_rows_sample.anchor: Team A says: "We know 95% of the system." Team B says: "We know 70% of the system." But Team B has discovered that there may be unknown dimensions. ... Team B may actually possess better epistemic knowledge, because it knows what it does not know. ... known unknowns vs. unknown unknowns. But your formulation is more precise because you're talking about dimensions of the ideal state, not merely missing facts.
a_rows_sample.statement: Extends the Team A/B example to a harder case: Team A claims 95% completeness with high confidence but low awareness of unknown dimensions, Team B claims only 70% completeness but has high awareness that unknown dimensions may exist; Team B may possess better epistemic knowledge because it knows what it does not know. Connects this to the known-unknowns/unknown-unknowns concept, but notes the present formulation is more precise since it concerns dimensions of the ideal state specifically, not merely missing facts in general.

a_rows_sample.anchor: A KnowledgeOS containing 10 million facts doesn't necessarily have more knowledge than one containing 1 million facts. ... Knowledge != Quantity of Information. Instead, at minimum: Knowledge ~ coverage of relevant dimensions + quality of information + confidence in completeness. Again, this is a research hypothesis, not yet a mathematical definition.
a_rows_sample.statement: Argues Knowledge cannot simply be measured by amount of stored information: a KnowledgeOS with 10 million facts about five dimensions need not have more knowledge than one with 1 million facts covering fifty dimensions -- Knowledge != Quantity of Information; instead, at minimum, Knowledge ~ coverage of relevant dimensions + quality of information + confidence in completeness, explicitly a research hypothesis, not yet a mathematical definition.

a_rows_sample.anchor: Level 1 -- Value uncertainty: Is the installed version 2.69 or 2.70? P(X=2.69|O). Level 2 -- Structural/dimensional uncertainty: Have we identified all relevant aspects of the system? P(dimension coverage is complete|O). The second is much harder. And this is precisely where I would now be very careful about saying "measure theory solves it." ... we first need to establish what the random object actually is.
a_rows_sample.statement: Splits probability into two levels: Level 1, value uncertainty (e.g. P(X=2.69|O) -- is the installed version 2.69 or 2.70), and Level 2, structural/dimensional uncertainty (P(dimension coverage is complete|O) -- have all relevant aspects of the system been identified), the second being much harder; warns against casually claiming 'measure theory solves it' for Level 2 before establishing what the underlying random object actually is.

a_rows_sample.anchor: the observer may also need to estimate: D the space of dimensions in which that state should be described. So the problem becomes: First discover the relevant state space and then: Estimate the state within that space. ... Now we may need: P(D,X|O) where D=what dimensions are relevant; X=what values those dimensions have.
a_rows_sample.statement: Generalizes P(X|O) to P(D,X|O): an observer must jointly estimate the relevant dimension space D and the values X within it, not merely X alone -- first discover the relevant state space, then estimate the state within that space -- a much richer epistemic problem than previously formulated.

a_rows_sample.anchor: C_fact: confidence that a particular determination is correct. C_coverage: confidence that we have identified the relevant dimensions. C_model: confidence that our model of how those dimensions relate is correct. These are three different uncertainties.
a_rows_sample.statement: Separates three distinct confidence types that a single '90-95%' figure conflates: C_fact (confidence a particular determination is correct), C_coverage (confidence the relevant dimensions have been identified), and C_model (confidence the model of how those dimensions relate is correct).

a_rows_sample.anchor: IDEAL STATE -> (potentially many/infinite dimensions) -> Dimension discovery -> Which dimensions do we believe are relevant? -> State extraction -> What is the value/state of each known dimension? -> Determination -> KNOWLEDGE. And probability may potentially operate at both discovery and extraction levels.
a_rows_sample.statement: Gives a pipeline diagram: IDEAL STATE (potentially many/infinite dimensions) -> Dimension discovery (which dimensions do we believe are relevant?) -> State extraction (what is the value/state of each known dimension?) -> Determination -> KNOWLEDGE; probability may operate at both the discovery and the extraction levels.

a_rows_sample.anchor: Not simply: "How accurately can we determine the state?" but: "How do we determine both the relevant dimensions of an ideal state and the state of those dimensions, given limited observation and reasoning capacity?" ... Dimension uncertainty + Value uncertainty + Temporal change + Comparative determination -- before we make any claim about what the KnowledgeOS Kernel must contain.
a_rows_sample.statement: Revises the central research question from 'how accurately can we determine the state?' to 'how do we determine both the relevant dimensions of an ideal state and the state of those dimensions, given limited observation and reasoning capacity?'; sets the research concentration as Dimension uncertainty + Value uncertainty + Temporal change + Comparative determination, explicitly before any claim about what the KnowledgeOS Kernel must contain.

a_rows_sample.anchor: C_value: How confident are we about the values of known dimensions? C_coverage: How confident are we that we have identified the relevant dimensions? C_model: How confident are we that our model of relationships between those dimensions is correct? This suggests that "knowledge completeness" is not one number. It may be multidimensional.
a_rows_sample.statement: Restates dimension completeness as the newest and perhaps most important addition, formalizing three confidences C_value (values of known dimensions), C_coverage (identification of relevant dimensions), and C_model (correctness of the model of relationships between dimensions); suggests 'knowledge completeness' is not one number but potentially multidimensional -- a major insight, still a hypothesis.

a_rows_sample.anchor: The two hardest unresolved questions are now: 1. How is the relevant dimension space discovered? and: 2. What exactly constitutes a valid epistemic determination? I would research those two questions next. And only after that would I return to measure theory and ask: Which parts of this process genuinely require measure-theoretic probability, and which do not? That prevents us from making the mathematics drive the ontology.
a_rows_sample.statement: Names the two hardest unresolved questions to research next: (1) how is the relevant dimension space discovered, and (2) what exactly constitutes a valid epistemic determination; only after resolving those should the research return to measure theory and ask which parts of the process genuinely require measure-theoretic probability and which do not -- explicitly to prevent the mathematics from driving the ontology.

a_rows_sample.anchor: Q1: What exactly is a "state"? ... Q2: Is every fact a dimension? ... Q3: Can dimensions themselves change? ... S_t -> S_{t+1} vs. D_t -> D_{t+1} ... Q4: What determines relevance of a dimension? Relevance(d | Context, Question, Purpose, Rules). But this is a hypothesis, not a definition.
a_rows_sample.statement: Poses four unresolved questions about the state/dimension ontology: Q1 what exactly is a 'state' (physical/software/business-process/institutional/propositional/knowledge-state, and can it contain entities/relationships/events/rules/capabilities/intentions/constraints); Q2 is every fact a dimension, or is the dimension-value pair distinct from the dimension itself, and does every relationship constitute a separate dimension; Q3 can dimensions themselves change (distinguishing state change S_t->S_{t+1} from dimension-model change D_t->D_{t+1}); Q4 what determines the relevance of a dimension, hypothesized as Relevance(d | Context, Question, Purpose, Rules) but not yet a definition. All marked Status: Undefined.

b_rows_sample.anchor: Human first has/conceives an Ideal State ... IDEAL STATE -> EXPECTATIONS/CRITERIA -> OBSERVATION -> COMPARISON -> DETERMINATION -> FACT/KNOWLEDGE. That is a substantially different model from the one I was using before.
b_rows_sample.statement: Major reorientation: humans do not build up an ideal state from arbitrary observations; instead a human first has/conceives an Ideal State and then evaluates reality against it, giving the pipeline IDEAL STATE -> EXPECTATIONS/CRITERIA -> OBSERVATION -> COMPARISON -> DETERMINATION -> FACT/KNOWLEDGE, substantially reversing the previously-used observation-first model.

b_rows_sample.anchor: Ideal state ... The complete state of what is supposed to be known/true/valid for the thing at that point in time. ... all applicable rules; all required participants; ... I_t = Ideal Knowledge State at t ... O_t -- comparison with I_t --> K_t
b_rows_sample.statement: Defines the ideal state I_t broadly as the complete state of what is supposed to be known/true/valid for a thing at time t; for an election system this would include all applicable rules, required participants, required conditions, valid relationships, required evidence, expected states, constraints, applicable laws, and known principles; every new piece of observed information O_t is evaluated against I_t, giving the extraction problem O_t --comparison with I_t--> K_t.

b_rows_sample.anchor: Information that correctly describes some aspect of the ideal state is Knowledge. ... K_t subset I_t ... The ideal state itself may be unknown to us. ... I_t -- the theoretical ideal state, and hat-I_t -- our current extracted/estimated representation of it. Then: hat-I_t != I_t in general. That may actually explain your earlier statement: "We try our best but never achieve the best."
b_rows_sample.statement: Refines 'information on the ideal state is knowledge' to 'information that correctly describes some aspect of the ideal state is Knowledge', giving K_t subset-or-equal I_t as the established/identified portion of the ideal state -- but the ideal state I_t itself may be unknown to us, so we must distinguish the theoretical ideal state I_t from our current extracted/estimated representation hat-I_t, with hat-I_t != I_t in general, explaining 'we try our best but never achieve the best'.

b_rows_sample.anchor: P(x|O_{<=t},I_t^known) ... Probability is involved in extracting the ideal state from imperfect observations. Not: Knowledge=Probability. Instead: Probability models the uncertainty of our extraction of the ideal state.
b_rows_sample.statement: Locates probability's role: for an ideal-state element x, given incomplete and overlapping observations O_1..O_n we estimate P(x|O_{<=t},I_t^known); probability is involved in extracting the ideal state from imperfect observations, not in defining Knowledge -- probability models the uncertainty of our extraction of the ideal state, not Knowledge itself.

b_rows_sample.anchor: System must have backup capability ... backup configuration exists ... If the applicable reasoning rules determine that the observation satisfies the criterion, we establish: F_t: "System has backup capability." ... the fact is not produced merely from the observation. It is produced by: Observation + Ideal State + Comparison Criteria + Reasoning.
b_rows_sample.statement: Worked example of fact production: ideal state I_t requires 'system must have backup capability', observation O_t is 'backup configuration exists'; comparing O_t against I_t via applicable reasoning rules establishes fact F_t='System has backup capability' -- a fact is produced not merely from observation but from Observation + Ideal State + Comparison Criteria + Reasoning together.

b_rows_sample.anchor: Logic = mechanism for comparing/deriving consequences from the ideal state and observed state. ... I_t: A and B and C. Observed: O_t: A,B,not-C. Logic gives: O_t does not entail I_t. Therefore the determination might be: F_t: "Current state does not satisfy the ideal state."
b_rows_sample.statement: Defines logic's role as the mechanism for comparing/deriving consequences from the ideal state and observed state: given ideal state I_t=(A and B and C) and observed O_t=(A,B,not-C), logic determines O_t does not entail I_t, yielding determination F_t='Current state does not satisfy the ideal state'.

b_rows_sample.anchor: P(A)=1, P(B)=0.9, P(C)=0.6, P(D)=0.2. Then our extracted representation of the ideal/current relationship is uncertain. The probability is therefore attached to the extraction/determination, not necessarily to the underlying ideal state itself. That gives: I_t -> hat-I_t where hat-I_t is probabilistically estimated from available information.
b_rows_sample.statement: Explains the origin of graded 0-to-1 values: if the ideal state requires A,B,C,D but observations only partially resolve them (P(A)=1,P(B)=0.9,P(C)=0.6,P(D)=0.2), the extracted representation of the ideal/current relationship is uncertain -- this probability attaches to the extraction/determination I_t -> hat-I_t, not to the underlying ideal state itself.

b_rows_sample.anchor: Where does the Ideal State come from? ... A. Given by reality I_t=Reality_t B. Given by human knowledge I_t=HumanModel_t C. Given by rules/laws/principles I_t=NormativeModel_t D. Given by the domain model I_t=DomainModel_t E. An ideal mathematical state I_t=I* F. Some combination I_t=f(Reality,Rules,Principles,Domain,HumanKnowledge). We should not assume which one it is.
b_rows_sample.statement: Poses 'Where does the Ideal State come from?' as, in the author's opinion, the most important unresolved problem, with six unassumed candidate sources: given by reality (I_t=Reality_t), given by human knowledge (I_t=HumanModel_t), given by rules/laws/principles (I_t=NormativeModel_t), given by the domain model (I_t=DomainModel_t), an ideal mathematical state (I_t=I*), or some combination I_t=f(Reality,Rules,Principles,Domain,HumanKnowledge) -- explicitly: we should not assume which one it is.

b_rows_sample.anchor: Knowledge = identified elements/relationships of an ideal state. And the current Knowledge state is K_t while the ideal state is I_t. The goal of knowledge extraction could therefore be: K_t -> I_t or more realistically: K_t approx I_t with the difference I_t - K_t representing what remains unknown, uncertain, or unextracted.
b_rows_sample.statement: Resolves 'is Knowledge a collection of facts?' into a richer formulation: Knowledge = identified elements/relationships of an ideal state; with current knowledge state K_t and ideal state I_t, knowledge extraction aims at K_t -> I_t or more realistically K_t approx I_t, with the residual I_t - K_t representing what remains unknown, uncertain, or unextracted.

b_rows_sample.anchor: "Every information on the ideal state of anything is knowledge." I would change "every information" to "every correctly determined proposition about the ideal state". ... "I believe the ideal state contains X." That is information about someone's belief, not necessarily Knowledge about the ideal state. ... "The document says X." ... Information about an ideal state != Knowledge of the ideal state.
b_rows_sample.statement: Challenges the overbroad claim 'every information on the ideal state of anything is knowledge', proposing instead 'every correctly determined proposition about the ideal state'; example: 'I believe the ideal state contains X' is information about someone's belief, not Knowledge about the ideal state, and 'the document says X' is knowledge that the document says X, not knowledge that X is true. Preserves the distinction: Information about an ideal state != Knowledge of the ideal state.

b_rows_sample.anchor: IDEAL STATE -> (defines expected/relevant structure) -> OBSERVED REALITY -> INFORMATION -> EXTRACTION -> (evidence/uncertainty) -> COMPARISON (ideal <-> observed) -> LOGIC -> DETERMINATION -> FACTS -> KNOWLEDGE STATE -> update over time. ... Probability primarily helps with the extraction from imperfect information, while Logic helps determine consequences and relationships.
b_rows_sample.statement: Gives the full revised pipeline diagram: IDEAL STATE (defines expected/relevant structure) -> OBSERVED REALITY -> INFORMATION -> EXTRACTION (branching into evidence and uncertainty) -> COMPARISON (ideal<->observed) -> LOGIC -> DETERMINATION -> FACTS -> KNOWLEDGE STATE -> update over time; probability primarily helps with extraction from imperfect information, logic helps determine consequences and relationships.

b_rows_sample.anchor: before determination, we now need to investigate: What is the Ideal State? Because determination is: D_t = Compare(Observed_t, Ideal_t) and if we don't understand Ideal_t, we don't fully understand D_t. ... IDEAL STATE -> OBSERVATION -> EXTRACTION -> COMPARISON -> DETERMINATION -> FACT -> KNOWLEDGE
b_rows_sample.statement: Revises the research direction: before determination can be understood, 'What is the Ideal State?' must be investigated, since determination is formalized as D_t=Compare(Observed_t,Ideal_t) and understanding D_t requires understanding Ideal_t; sets the research sequence as IDEAL STATE -> OBSERVATION -> EXTRACTION -> COMPARISON -> DETERMINATION -> FACT -> KNOWLEDGE, with Probability->uncertain extraction and Logic->comparison and consequence.

b_rows_sample.anchor: the fundamental question for KnowledgeOS is not "How do we store Knowledge?" and not even "How do we extract Knowledge?" It may be: "How is an ideal state of Knowledge defined, and how does a system continuously determine its current relationship to that ideal state?" ... Knowledge becomes the currently justified representation of the relationship between them. I would now research Ideal State / normative state / complete state / target state / possible-world state / domain model / epistemic idealization across mathematics, epistemology, AI, systems theory, DDD, and philosophy before we touch the Kernel again.
b_rows_sample.statement: States what may be 'the biggest discovery so far': the fundamental KnowledgeOS question may be neither 'how do we store Knowledge' nor 'how do we extract Knowledge' but 'how is an ideal state of Knowledge defined, and how does a system continuously determine its current relationship to that ideal state?'; Knowledge becomes the currently justified representation of the relationship between Ideal State and Observed State. Proposes researching Ideal State / normative state / complete state / target state / possible-world state / domain model / epistemic idealization across mathematics, epistemology, AI, systems theory, DDD, and philosophy before returning to Kernel definition.

b_rows_sample.anchor: "Every information" you mean all possible information about the thing, not merely "some information." So your proposition is: I_t = the totality of all possible information about the object/domain at time t. And I_t may be infinite.
b_rows_sample.statement: Reinterprets 'every information' as meaning ALL possible information about a thing, not merely some information: I_t is redefined as the totality of all possible information about the object/domain at time t, and I_t may be infinite -- a much stronger interpretation than given previously.

b_rows_sample.anchor: O_t subset I_t or, more realistically, imperfect projections of I_t. The extraction process is therefore: I_t -> observable information -> extracted knowledge, with the extraction being imperfect because the underlying elements can overlap and the observation process cannot completely distinguish them.
b_rows_sample.statement: A human/system cannot access all of the (possibly infinite) I_t, only observations O_t subset I_t or imperfect projections of it; extraction is I_t -> observable information -> extracted knowledge, imperfect because underlying elements can overlap and observation cannot completely distinguish them.

b_rows_sample.anchor: K = the space of all possible information/knowledge elements ... I_t subset K is the complete/ideal information state relevant at that time. Then an observer A has only an extracted state: K_t^A subset I_t ... K_t^A != I_t in general.
b_rows_sample.statement: Sharpens 'Knowledge is a state and subset of elements of the infinite Knowledge Space' into: K-script (the space of all possible information/knowledge elements), with I_t subset K-script being the complete/ideal information state relevant at time t; an observer A has only an extracted state K_t^A subset I_t (or a representation/projection of it), and because extraction is imperfect, K_t^A != I_t in general.

b_rows_sample.anchor: P(x in I_t | O_{<=t}^A). So probability describes the extraction uncertainty. ... Knowledge itself is not probability. Rather: Probability can describe the imperfect extraction of Knowledge from the ideal information state.
b_rows_sample.statement: For an ideal-state element x in I_t that an observer cannot directly verify, the observer estimates P(x in I_t | O_{<=t}^A) given its observations -- probability describes extraction uncertainty, consistent with 'the elements overlap and only probability can extract them as separately as possible' (still to be tested as the right mathematical mechanism, but a coherent hypothesis). Knowledge itself is not probability; probability describes the imperfect extraction of Knowledge from the ideal information state.

b_rows_sample.anchor: If I_t means all possible information, then we need to distinguish: possible information from true information and knowable information. ... whether your I_t means: 1. all logically possible information, or 2. all information that is actually true about the thing at t, or 3. all information that could in principle be known about the thing at t. I think this distinction is now the next critical question.
b_rows_sample.statement: Raises the next critical question: since not every possible description of a system is true, I_t must be disambiguated among three readings -- (1) all logically possible information, (2) all information that is actually true about the thing at t, or (3) all information that could in principle be known about the thing at t; this distinction will determine the meaning of the 'infinite Knowledge Space' and what KnowledgeOS is trying to extract from it.

b_rows_sample.anchor: I_t = the potentially infinite space of all relevant states/propositions/relationships at time t ... K_t (script) = Infinite Knowledge Space at t and I_t subset K_t (script) could represent an ideal state/configuration of the domain. But even I_t may itself be infinite. ... K_t = Pi_t(I_t) where Pi_t is the extraction/projection available to the observer.
b_rows_sample.statement: If I_t can be infinite, it should not be modeled as a finite list of facts but as the potentially infinite space of all relevant states/propositions/relationships at t; introduces K-script_t (infinite Knowledge Space at t) with I_t subset K-script_t as an ideal state/configuration of the domain (itself possibly infinite), and the observer's actual accessible/extracted knowledge as K_t subset I_t or, more generally, K_t=Pi_t(I_t) where Pi_t is the observer's extraction/projection function.

b_rows_sample.anchor: I_t={x_1,x_2,x_3,...}. We cannot observe all of them. ... construct an estimate hat-I_t from the observations. For an element x: P(x in I_t | O_{<=t},C_t) can express our uncertainty ... probability is increasingly looking like a mathematics of extraction from an incompletely observable/infinite state, rather than a definition of Knowledge.
b_rows_sample.statement: With an infinite ideal state I_t={x_1,x_2,...} that cannot be fully observed, an estimate hat-I_t is constructed from observations O_{<=t}, and for an element x, P(x in I_t | O_{<=t},C_t) expresses uncertainty about membership; probability is increasingly a mathematics of extraction from an incompletely observable/infinite state, not a definition of Knowledge.

b_notations: IDEAL STATE -> OBSERVATION -> EXTRACTION -> COMPARISON -> DETERMINATION -> FACT -> KNOWLEDGE

a_rows_sample.anchor: What would it mean to build against this architecture? Honestly: mostly future work, and this chapter will not pretend otherwise.
a_rows_sample.statement: Explicit framing: building against this architecture is mostly future work; the chapter states this honestly rather than overstating implementation maturity.

a_rows_sample.anchor: a session bootstrap that resolves a process's lane, role, and authority from the governed record and *fails closed* — on any unresolved fact the answer is "not authorized," never a guess ... None of the formal objects — the gap function, the contract derivation, the ladder as datatype, the decision
a_rows_sample.statement: What exists today: a fail-closed session bootstrap (any unresolved fact answers 'not authorized', never a guess), a read-only presenter of the adopted operating model, and observation-pipeline diagnostics that only check and report, never install or repair. None of the formal objects (gap function, contract derivation, ladder-as-datatype, decision contract) has any implementation.

a_rows_sample.anchor: An engineering programme that wanted them would start from the ratified signatures in Part III and would inherit twelve open questions, two of which (the aggregation operator, OQ-3; action semantics, OQ-4) sit directly on the implementation path.
a_rows_sample.statement: Any engineering programme implementing the formal objects would start from Part III's ratified signatures and inherit all twelve open questions, two of which (OQ-3 the aggregation operator; OQ-4 action semantics) sit directly on the implementation path.

a_rows_sample.anchor: duplicates must not raise confidence and dependency resolution precedes aggregation (the two TESTED rows are the two an evidence store cannot skip); admission must pass a versioned in-force policy; commitment must be an authority act distinct from acceptance; skipping statuses must be structurally i
a_rows_sample.statement: The invariants read as an implementation specification: an evidence store cannot skip duplicate-suppression or dependency-first aggregation (the two TESTED invariants); admission must pass a versioned in-force policy; commitment must be a distinct authority act from acceptance; status-skipping must be structurally impossible; and the state store must hold rejection, conflict, and ignorance as first-class conditions rather than deleting them.

a_rows_sample.anchor: govern the *authority* layer first. The bootstrap implements no epistemics at all — only the refusal to conflate identity with authorization — and it is already the strongest implementation-side evidence the conformance pass found for anything. ... the boundaries are cheaper than the calculus, and t
a_rows_sample.statement: Recommended adoption pattern: govern the authority layer first, as the session-bootstrap tooling does (no epistemics implemented, only the refusal to conflate identity with authorization) -- already the strongest implementation-side evidence the conformance pass found for anything; boundaries are cheaper to build than the calculus and the architecture's history suggests they matter more.

a_rows_sample.anchor: Nothing on the repository side states the dependency-first ordering rule (I-6). Any implementation of evidence handling should carry that sentence in its contract before it carries any code.
a_rows_sample.statement: OQ-12: nothing on the repository side states the dependency-first ordering rule (invariant I-6); any future implementation of evidence handling should carry that sentence in its contract before it carries any code.

b_rows_sample.anchor: A_n = 1.00000 F_n = 1.00000 published run reported F_n = 1.0 at R5 -> REPRODUCED => adequate AND F=1: the published design excluded its own target by construction.
b_rows_sample.statement: The control frame (Q,C,O) reproduces the published F_n=1.00000 result exactly, confirming the published experiment's design (adequate representation with perfect realization) as reproduced before testing the two witness routes.

b_rows_sample.anchor: ROUTE 1 -- frame (Q,C,O_weak): F_n = 0.52065, argmax component = 0.52065 (where O_weak is weaker), decile component = 1.00000 (unchanged by construction). Hhat(Q|R)=0.00000 AND F=0.52065<1 -> WITNESS FOUND

b_rows_sample.anchor: ROUTE 2 -- frame (Q, C and k-anonymity(k=2), O): A_n (with k-anon) = 0.57652, cases blocked = 16939 (42.35%), F_n = 0.57652. Hhat(Q|R)=0.00000 AND F=0.57652<1 -> WITNESS FOUND. singleton fibers = 16939 of 26826.

a_rows_sample.anchor: Goal\neq EpistemicContract
a_rows_sample.statement: A goal (e.g. 'Migrate Nexus to the target architecture') does not itself contain all knowledge conditions necessary to execute it safely (e.g. RollbackVerified, FirewallRequirementsKnown are not stated by the goal); therefore Goal ≠ EpistemicContract. States this was already discovered in Step 25D and now needs formalizing.

a_rows_sample.anchor: DeriveContract(G,S)\rightarrow EC_G
a_rows_sample.statement: Defines the conceptual operation DeriveContract(G,S) -> EC_G, where S is the set of governing sources {Constitution, Policy, ADR, Rule, Scope, HumanInstruction, RiskModel, DomainModel, Law, Standard}.

a_rows_sample.anchor: EC\in KnowledgeState
a_rows_sample.statement: The epistemic contract EC is itself an artifact needing identity, version, scope, owner, source, derivation, validity period, authority, and status; therefore EC ∈ KnowledgeState — 'the system needs knowledge to define what knowledge is required.'

a_rows_sample.anchor: EC=(R,\Gamma,A,V)
a_rows_sample.statement: First contract tuple definition: EC=(R,Γ,A,V) where R=requirements, Γ=satisfaction rules, A=authority/provenance, V=validity/version; R={r1,...,rn}, each requirement individually traceable (e.g. r1: RollbackVerified derived via MigrationGoal -> ArchitecturePolicy -> RiskRule -> RollbackVerified).

a_rows_sample.anchor: RequirementLineage
a_rows_sample.statement: Defines RequirementLineage: a traceable derivation tree from Goal through governing artifacts (Architecture Constitution, Security Policy, Migration Risk Rule) to a concrete requirement (Rollback Verification), enabling the system to answer 'why does KnowledgeOS require a rollback test?' with a traced derivation rather than 'the AI thought it was important.'

a_rows_sample.anchor: HumanInstruction\rightarrow Goal/Intent. Then Goal+Governance\rightarrow Contract.
a_rows_sample.statement: A human instruction (e.g. 'Please migrate Nexus next weekend') contributes only Intent/Goal, not an automatic requirement like RollbackVerifiedRequired; requirements arise from Goal+Governance -> Contract, which 'prevents instructions from silently becoming rules.'

a_rows_sample.anchor: Scope=Production... A requirement concerning a development Nexus instance may therefore be NotApplicable
a_rows_sample.statement: Scope must be an explicit contract dimension: a requirement scoped to Production is NotApplicable to a development instance, demonstrated via example.

a_rows_sample.anchor: Suppose the architecture constitution says: Production changes require architectural assurance... r_{architecture-assurance} becomes part of R_G
a_rows_sample.statement: A constitution-derived requirement (architecture-assurance) is 'not an opinion' but a normative consequence of the constitution, illustrating Constitution -> Requirement derivation.

a_rows_sample.anchor: ADR\rightarrow Requirement
a_rows_sample.statement: An ADR fixing TargetArchitecture=ContainerizedNexusPro can satisfy TargetArchitectureKnown if authoritative/current, and may also generate additional derived requirements (e.g. r_container-security) from the target architecture's own security constraints — ADR -> Requirement.

a_rows_sample.anchor: Suppose a risk analysis identifies RISK: DataLoss... The contract can derive RollbackVerified. This is important because the requirement may not come directly from an architecture rule. It may emerge from Goal+Risk.
a_rows_sample.statement: A risk-model-derived requirement path: RISK:DataLoss -> Control:VerifiedRestore -> RollbackVerified, showing requirements can emerge from Goal+Risk rather than only from architecture rules.

a_rows_sample.anchor: CandidateRequirement\neq ContractRequirement
a_rows_sample.statement: Distinguishes valid derivation (Source+Rule -> Requirement) from mere AI suggestion (LLM -> CandidateRequirement): the latter is not automatically binding, giving 'another deterministic assurance boundary': CandidateRequirement ≠ ContractRequirement.

a_rows_sample.anchor: SourceExists? SourceApplicable? AuthorityValid? RuleSatisfied? ... CandidateRequirement\rightarrow ContractRequirement
a_rows_sample.statement: Describes the LLM's role as proposing candidate requirements from unstructured sources (e.g. reading a 300-page policy), which KnowledgeOS records as CandidateRequirement; only after a deterministic/governed check (SourceExists?, SourceApplicable?, AuthorityValid?, RuleSatisfied?) does CandidateRequirement -> ContractRequirement.

a_rows_sample.anchor: Knowledge requirement / Evidence requirement / Validation requirement / Governance requirement / Operational requirement
a_rows_sample.statement: Introduces a five-way requirement-type taxonomy with predicate forms and examples: Knowledge requirement Known(r) (e.g. TargetVersionKnown), Evidence requirement EvidenceExists(r) (e.g. BackupEvidenceAvailable), Validation requirement Validated(r) (e.g. RestoreTestPassed), Governance requirement Authorized(r) (e.g. ArchitectureApprovalGranted), Operational requirement State(r) (e.g. TargetEnvironmentProvisioned).

a_rows_sample.anchor: Epistemic-Governance Contract ... or simply AssuranceContract. I would not rename it yet
a_rows_sample.statement: Because the requirement taxonomy now spans Knowledge+Evidence+Validation+Authorization+State rather than only 'what must be known,' proposes the more precise terms 'Epistemic-Governance Contract' or 'AssuranceContract,' but explicitly declines to rename yet since 'Epistemic Contract' retains conceptual value — records the naming issue rather than resolving it.

a_rows_sample.anchor: EC_{Nexus}=\{r_1,\ldots,r_8\}
a_rows_sample.statement: Worked example contract for Nexus with an 8-row requirement table (current version known, target architecture known, repository inventory verified, backup verified, rollback verified, network requirements resolved, security assessment complete, architecture approval), each tagged by Type and Blocking?=Yes, giving 'Zero something precise to evaluate.'

a_rows_sample.anchor: r_1\land r_2\Rightarrow r_3 ... r_4\lor r_5
a_rows_sample.statement: Requirements may have logical relations: conjunction (BackupExists AND RestoreTestPassed => RollbackCapabilityEstablished) and disjunction (either approved rollback procedure A OR B suffices), concluding 'EpistemicContract is a constraint system.'

a_rows_sample.anchor: BackupExists ... RestoreValidated ... RollbackVerified ... MigrationEligible
a_rows_sample.statement: Requirement dependency graph diagram lets Zero determine not just which requirements are unmet but 'which gap blocks downstream requirements' — e.g. if BackupExists=Unknown, RestoreValidated and RollbackVerified cannot be established, so RootGap=BackupExists rather than three unrelated gaps; described as 'much more efficient' and 'extremely useful for Lord.'

a_rows_sample.anchor: Closed(EC)
a_rows_sample.statement: Defines contract closure: Closed(EC) holds if every requirement has a semantic definition, an authority, a satisfaction rule, applicable scope, validity, and dependency definition; otherwise Closed(EC)=False, becoming 'another assurance gate.'

a_rows_sample.anchor: UndefinedRequirement\Rightarrow InvalidContract
a_rows_sample.statement: An AI-created requirement like r9: SystemMustBe"HighlySecure" with no satisfaction predicate makes Evaluate(K,r9) non-deterministic; therefore UndefinedRequirement => InvalidContract — 'the contract is defective.'

a_rows_sample.anchor: Contract normalization: natural-language sources normalized into canonical requirements like RollbackProcedureExists and RollbackProcedureTested; natural language remains provenance
a_rows_sample.statement: Describes contract normalization: an LLM can help normalize vague natural-language sources ('Make sure the migration is safe') into canonical, structured, executable requirements while the natural language remains provenance.

b_rows_sample.anchor: distinguish computable from computationally expensive and from requiring external capabilities
b_rows_sample.statement: Opens the file (before the Step 25F heading) answering a user question by proposing the order of investigation ('25F first, then test the architecture against a normal PC') and distinguishing three separate questions: computable, computationally expensive, and requiring external capabilities.

b_rows_sample.anchor: Constitution\vdash r ... ADR_17\vdash\neg r ... approval = true + false
b_rows_sample.statement: The fundamental motivating example: a Constitution requiring Architecture Board approval for production changes conflicts with an old ADR saying approval is not required; naively collecting both as 'approval = true + false' is rejected — the system must determine whether the contradiction is resolvable by the governance model.

b_rows_sample.anchor: Conflict \neq Error
b_rows_sample.statement: First principle: two contradicting statements are not automatically an error — they may (1) have one superseding the other, (2) apply to different scopes, (3) apply at different times, (4) involve an exception, (5) reflect different authority, (6) have one simply invalid, or (7) reflect genuine unresolved governance conflict. Therefore Conflict ≠ Error; conflict is 'an input state requiring resolution.'

b_rows_sample.anchor: Scope(A)\cap Scope(B)=\varnothing \Rightarrow Conflict(A,B)=False
b_rows_sample.statement: Scope precedes conflict: Policy_A:r for Production and Policy_B:¬r for Development do not conflict because Scope(A)∩Scope(B)=∅, giving the governance rule: before resolving contradiction, determine whether the propositions actually apply to the same context.

b_rows_sample.anchor: Policy_A: r, t<2026 ... Policy_B: \neg r, t\ge 2026 ... Conflict=False
b_rows_sample.statement: Temporal applicability similarly dissolves apparent conflict: time-disjoint policies produce Conflict=False for any given evaluation time t; conflict detection must first evaluate Applicable(s,C,t).

b_rows_sample.anchor: Conflict(s_1,s_2,C,t) ... Applicable(s_1,C,t) and Applicable(s_2,C,t) and Conclusion(s_1)\neq Conclusion(s_2)
b_rows_sample.statement: Defines effective conflict formally: Conflict(s1,s2,C,t) holds only when both sources are Applicable(.,C,t) and their Conclusions differ — described as 'much cleaner' than a naive contradiction check.

type_signature.domain: Source x Source x Context x Time

b_rows_sample.anchor: Resolve(s_1,s_2,C,t) ... {s1 wins, s2 wins, both coexist, exception, superseded, unresolved}
b_rows_sample.statement: Defines a resolution relation Resolve(s1,s2,C,t) with six possible outcome categories: s1 wins, s2 wins, both coexist, exception, superseded, unresolved.

b_rows_sample.anchor: ADR_1\vdash r ... ADR_2\vdash\neg r ... ADR_2 supersedes ADR_1 ... Effective(ADR_1)=False ... HistoricalConflict\neq CurrentConflict
b_rows_sample.statement: Supersession example: when ADR_2 explicitly supersedes ADR_1, Effective(ADR_1)=False, so there is no active contradiction — the historical contradiction remains in KnowledgeOS history but 'does not contaminate current governance,' giving HistoricalConflict ≠ CurrentConflict.

b_rows_sample.anchor: Exception(r,C) ... r=True and ExceptionApplied=True ... SatisfiedByException
b_rows_sample.statement: Explicit exception handling: an authorized exception to a Constitution-required r should not delete r; instead the system records r=True and ExceptionApplied=True, giving state SatisfiedByException — 'preserves both the rule and the deviation.'

b_rows_sample.anchor: Requirement: Architecture approval required -> deleted because someone approved an exception ... destroys governance history
b_rows_sample.statement: Warns that silently deleting a requirement upon exception approval 'destroys governance history'; shows the correct representation retains the Requirement plus an Exception record (approver, scope, validity date) so the system can explain exactly why the normal requirement was not enforced in the ordinary way.

b_rows_sample.anchor: HumanInstruction\vdash\neg r ... Authority(HumanInstruction)<Authority(Constitution) ... EffectiveConclusion=r ... Rejected/NonBinding
b_rows_sample.statement: If an unauthorized human instruction contradicts the Constitution and Authority(HumanInstruction) < Authority(Constitution), the EffectiveConclusion remains r and the human instruction becomes Rejected/NonBinding (though it should remain recorded).

b_rows_sample.anchor: HumanDecision\rightarrow AuthorizedException ... Instruction ... AuthorizedDecision
b_rows_sample.statement: Distinguishes two semantic categories of 'human instruction': a mere Instruction versus an AuthorizedDecision from an authorized governance authority explicitly granting an exception (HumanDecision -> AuthorizedException), showing 'human instruction' is not one uniform category.

b_rows_sample.anchor: AIOutput\vdash\neg r ... Binding(AIOutput)=False ... AIOutput cannot directly override governance
b_rows_sample.statement: AI-generated governance claims (e.g. an LLM asserting an approval is unnecessary) are not binding unless backed by an authoritative source and accepted through the governance mechanism: Binding(AIOutput)=False, and 'AIOutput cannot directly override governance' — 'a fundamental KnowledgeOS invariant.'

b_rows_sample.anchor: GovernanceResolve(C,S,t)\rightarrow GR ... GR=(EffectiveRules,Conflicts,Exceptions,Supersessions,UnresolvedItems)
b_rows_sample.statement: Defines the formal governance-resolution function GovernanceResolve(Context,Sources,time) -> GR, where GR is a five-component result tuple: EffectiveRules, Conflicts, Exceptions, Supersessions, UnresolvedItems.

b_rows_sample.anchor: S=\{Constitution,ADR_17,Policy_4,Exception_2\} ... Step1..Step7
b_rows_sample.statement: Worked example walking a seven-step engine process (determine applicability; normalize propositions; detect contradictions; apply supersession; apply authority; apply authorized exceptions; produce effective rules), described as 'computationally straightforward provided the governance semantics are explicitly modeled.'

b_rows_sample.anchor: Suppose two equally authoritative sources say r and \neg r. No precedence exists ... Resolve=Unresolved ... KnowledgeOS must not invent an answer
b_rows_sample.statement: The crucial boundary case: when two equally authoritative sources genuinely conflict with no precedence, Resolve=Unresolved and 'KnowledgeOS must not invent an answer' — therefore UnresolvedGovernanceConflict -> HumanGovernance, explicitly stated as 'not a failure of KnowledgeOS' but 'the correct computational result.'

b_rows_sample.anchor: whether the conflict is computationally resolvable ... Knowing that something cannot be determined is itself a valid computed result
b_rows_sample.statement: States what is called 'one of the most important conclusions so far': the kernel's job is not to solve every semantic conflict but to determine whether the conflict is computationally resolvable (Resolve if yes, Escalate if no) — 'Knowing that something cannot be determined is itself a valid computed result,' framed as a principle that 'will become important throughout the architecture.'

b_rows_sample.anchor: Resolved / Unresolved / Invalid
b_rows_sample.statement: Defines three fundamental governance-resolution outcome states: Resolved (a deterministic precedence/exception rule exists), Unresolved (valid sources conflict with no resolution mechanism), Invalid (a source or rule cannot legally/semantically participate).

b_rows_sample.anchor: Constitution: ProductionChange=>ArchitectureApproval ... ADR: NexusChange=>NoApproval ... GovernanceStatus=Unresolved ... Zero becomes ArchitectureApproval=Conflicted ... Lord should not guess
b_rows_sample.statement: Full worked example with no supersession/exception/scope-or-time distinction: GovernanceStatus=Unresolved, so Zero reports ArchitectureApproval=Conflicted, and Lord 'should not guess' — instead it generates the action ResolveGovernanceConflict.

b_rows_sample.anchor: GovernanceResolve(S, Context, Time): 1..9 steps
b_rows_sample.statement: Presents the full nine-step GovernanceResolve algorithm (filter by applicability; resolve versions; remove superseded; normalize propositions; detect contradictory conclusions; apply authority; apply authorized exceptions; determine effective rules; return unresolved conflicts) and states 'the difficult part is not computational complexity... it is making the semantics explicit.'

group_evidence.why_grouped: explicit agent-stated uncertainty: 'governance-conflict-resolution-algebra' POSSIBLY relates to 'epistemic-contract-derivation-algebra' (batch B0022). Note: S0898's Step 25F: resolves the conflict/authority gap flagged at the end of S0897 (Step 25E) via applicability-gated conflict detection, supersession, exceptions, a partial-order authority lattice, and Resolved/Unresolved/Invalid outcomes; also contains a distinct computability-of-the-kernel analysis (semantic vs computational bottleneck, kernel vs intelligence-layer separation).

a_rows_sample.anchor: I treated MD-058 and MD-059 as the frozen handover boundary and used only their recorded evidence/provenance and the primary corpus sources they explicitly relied upon. I did not perform new theory, reconciliation, model selection, F3<->F4 bridging, external literature research, or implementation. F4 is semantically instantiated in form, but not closed enough to make its satisfaction semantics computable; and it is not yet typed into a common observation space with F3. The two remaining blockers are therefore distinct: internal F4 closure and cross-model bridging.
a_rows_sample.statement: States the audit's decisive finding and self-imposed scope boundary: F4 is instantiated in form but not computationally closed, and separately not yet typed into a common observation space with F3 -- two genuinely distinct blockers (internal F4 closure vs cross-model bridging), both named by MD-059 as separate unauthorized next acts.

a_rows_sample.anchor: F4 completeness matrix A-K: A K_t variant census PARTIALLY FOUND (9+ mutually unreconciled variants, only 1 of 11 named components concretely typed); B component semantics NOT FOUND (only Sigma_t=(A,S,R,V,C) concretely defined, in one variant only); C relationships among variants CONFLICTING (mutually unreconciled, no component-level consistency established); D corpus-grounded common semantic core NOT FOUND; E R_t semantics PARTIALLY FOUND (Req(EC_t) exists as formal input but satisfaction predicates remain multiply defined/contested); F Sat(K_t,r) semantics PARTIALLY FOUND (shape frozen, but computing Sat requires K_t component semantics which are incomplete -- defined in form but not computationally closed); G decomposition-independent Sat NOT FOUND (the principal internal F4 blocker); H K_t->K_{t+1} transition semantics CONFLICTING (delta(K_t,e_t) and the P-12/P-13 family unresolved); I F4 Obs PARTIALLY FOUND (constructible in form, not computable); J F4 Beh PARTIALLY FOUND (general slot exists, no executable F4 Beh, classified UNAVAILABLE); K F4 Trace PARTIALLY FOUND (general machinery exists, no F4-specific instances).
a_rows_sample.statement: Gives the full eleven-item (A-K) F4 completeness matrix distinguishing what exists in form/shape from what is computationally closed across the K_t variant census, component semantics, R_t/Sat semantics, and F4's Obs/Beh/Trace, concluding this is why MD-059 did not describe F4 as simply absent -- the semantic shell is real but instantiation is incomplete.

a_rows_sample.anchor: F3<->F4 readiness matrix L-Q: L F3 observation semantics FOUND (Beh_c(K):=Reach(Ops(K)), the only candidate with real instantiated semantics); M F4 observation semantics PARTIALLY FOUND (formally constructible, not computable since Sat is not closed); N atoms<->requirements bridge NOT FOUND (F3 outputs reached atoms, F4 outputs satisfied requirements, no corpus document bridges these types); O common observation domain NOT FOUND (different codomains, no common Q,O can be posed without inventing the bridge); P common behaviour/trace domain NOT FOUND (F3 has instantiated behaviour, F4 does not); Q formal F3<->F4 equivalence relation NOT FOUND (MD-058 derived the general shape Obs-equality but not the corpus-intended ≡, and its cross-candidate matrix left all 15 pairs unresolved).
a_rows_sample.statement: Gives the full six-item (L-Q) F3<->F4 readiness matrix, establishing F3 as the only model with real instantiated observation semantics and F4 as merely formally constructible, with the critical N/O finding that F3 and F4 currently have no corpus-grounded bridge between their output types (atoms vs satisfied requirements) at all.

a_rows_sample.anchor: K1 approx_{Q,O} K2 iff Obs_{Q,O}(K1)=Obs_{Q,O}(K2). But this is not a completed F3<->F4 equivalence result. a_rows_sample.anchor: K_t in K-blackboard, K-blackboard = space of admissible semantic epistemic states. It explicitly refuses to make K_t universally equal to a tuple and instead distinguishes semantic state from representation. K_t=(Content,Support,Uncertainty,Model,Alternatives,History,Identity,Context,Inquiry,Status) but explicitly a semantic decomposition, not a mandatory storage tuple. a_rows_sample.statement: Establishes that the historical corpus defines K_t as an abstract semantic epistemic state (K_t in K-blackboard, deliberately not reduced to a mandatory tuple, with a ten-field semantic decomposition explicitly marked non-mandatory) alongside a separate, unselected 11-component concrete Model-B tuple family, verdict FOUND-UNTYPED for the abstract form and CONFLICTING for the concrete family, with no evidence selecting between the concrete formulations.

a_rows_sample.anchor: r(K_t)=x_t. Representation carrier (X_r, A_r) and family R-script={R_r: r in R}, R_r: K-blackboard <-> X_r. No single representation is automatically the KnowledgeOS ontology. Notation collision: in representation theory r denotes a representation; in gap theory r denotes an epistemic requirement r=(id,type,scope,content,standard,priority,validity). The corpus does not establish that these two uses of r are the same object.
a_rows_sample.statement: Establishes the representation function r(K_t)=x_t with a representation carrier and family, explicitly noting no representation is automatically canonical, but leaves the mathematical type of r, its totality/injectivity/invertibility properties, and x_t's precise type unclosed; identifies a genuine notation collision where 'r' denotes a representation in one theory and a seven-field epistemic requirement in another, with the corpus never establishing these are the same object. Verdict: FOUND-UNTYPED.

There is no historical rule showing that Obs_F4(K_t) is obtained from r(K_t)=x_t, from EC, or from Sat. Verdict: Generic Obs FOUND-TYPED; F4-specific Obs_F4 NOT FOUND.
a_rows_sample.statement: Finds a generic, formally typed historical Obs function (O_t^s=Obs(s,W_t,m_t,c_t)) but no rule deriving an F4-specific Obs_F4 from any of r(K_t), EC, or Sat, verdict: generic Obs FOUND-TYPED, F4-specific Obs_F4 NOT FOUND.

Missing: contract structure present; contract construction algorithm absent; fully grounded Sat only partial. No source establishes that EC_t is identical to C_KOS. a_rows_sample.statement: Establishes the epistemic contract EC_t=EC(S_t,G_t,Q_t,C_t) with its role in defining an admissible ideal region and adequacy, but finds no construction algorithm for EC_t and no evidence that EC_t is identical to C_KOS (the two should remain separate concepts), verdict FOUND-UNTYPED.

a_rows_sample.anchor: The ten Sat questions -- decisive audit: 1. Domain of K_t? K-blackboard proposed, exact structure OPEN. 2. Type of r? seven-field tuple proposed. 3. Codomain? {0,1} explicitly proposed; competing top/bot/U sub-semantics also exist. 4. Total/partial? NOT ESTABLISHED. 5. Evidence required? categories discussed, no complete evaluator. 6. Meaning of 1? requirement satisfied. 7. Meaning of 0? requirement unsatisfied. 8. Insufficient evidence? NOT CLOSED, candidate Unknown semantics exist. 9. Is UNKNOWN distinct? general theory yes, F4 Sat treatment NOT ESTABLISHED. 10. Deterministic/reproducible? NO -- no complete evaluation algorithm. Two engineers cannot currently compute the same Sat(K_t,r) from corpus-defined rules alone.
a_rows_sample.statement: Runs a ten-question decisive audit of Sat(K_t,r) against the historical corpus, finding the codomain itself contested (binary {0,1} vs a ternary top/bot/Unknown sub-semantics with no authorized selection), totality/evidence-sufficiency/insufficient-evidence-treatment all unclosed, and concludes with a definitive negative reproducibility test: two engineers cannot currently compute the same Sat(K_t,r) result from corpus-defined rules alone.

a_rows_sample.anchor: Delta_t = {r in R_t: Sat(K_t,r)=0}. It is the strongest historical F4 formula and was subsequently frozen as a constraint. R_t typed? PARTIALLY/candidate-typed. Sat typed? PARTIALLY; codomain conflicting. Sat executable? NO. Delta_t formula defined? YES. Delta_t executable? NO. Therefore: defined Delta_t != computable Delta_t. Verdict: Delta_t FOUND-UNTYPED as an operational object. The set-formula exists, but its evaluation cannot yet be executed.
a_rows_sample.statement: Confirms Delta_t's set-builder formula is the strongest, frozen historical F4 formula, but derives via a five-row dependency table that it is not executable since Sat is not executable, establishing the sharp distinction defined Delta_t != computable Delta_t.

a_rows_sample.anchor: Transition semantics: K_{t+1}=T(K_t,E_{t+1},Q_t,C_t,EC_t,A_t) and H_{t+1}=H_t union {transition_t}; also K_{t+1}=Transition(K_t,Operation,Parameters) with remaining work to define exact operation semantics/pre/postconditions; also H_t=(e_0,...,e_{t-1}), H_{t+1}=H_t || e_t, Replay(K_0,H_t)=K_t. These must not be collapsed: T, delta, Transition, event-based, operation-based, history, replay are not established as one formally identical transition system. The later persistence audit explicitly records that the tau_1..tau_11 items are transition CLASSES, not functions. Do not equate the tau classes with delta.
a_rows_sample.statement: Catalogs at least four distinct historical transition-semantics formulations (T-based, event-based Transition/Operation, history-append with Replay, and tau_1..tau_11 transition classes) and explicitly warns against collapsing them into one formally identical transition system, particularly against equating the tau classes (transition classes, not functions) with delta.

b_rows_sample.anchor: Define -> Prove -> Falsify -> Validate -> Freeze -- not: Define everything -> implement. I would structure the remaining work into 9 theory gates. T1 Ontological boundaries Strong; T2 Knowledge State K_t Ratified; T3 Proposition+Evidence+Inquiry Developed; T4 Requirement+Satisfaction Open; T5 Knowledge Gap+Zero Partially defined; T6 Transformation+Preservation Developed; T7 State Transition+History Open; T8 Semantic Equivalence Open; T9 Decision/Action+F3<->F4 Open. T4-T8 are not independent.
b_rows_sample.statement: Proposes a Define->Prove->Falsify->Validate->Freeze discipline applied gate-by-gate (rather than defining the whole theory before implementing), organizing remaining work into nine theory gates T1-T9 each with a current status and explicit interdependency among T4-T8.

b_rows_sample.anchor: Step 1 -- Freeze the theoretical vocabulary. Reality != Observation != Information != Representation != Proposition != Evidence != Knowledge != Determination != Decision != Action. For every concept ask: What is it? What is it not? What inputs does it take? What outputs does it produce? What is its epistemic status? Is it corpus-derived or newly proposed? This becomes the Theory Vocabulary Constitution. Do not add new primitives until this is done.
b_rows_sample.statement: Proposes Gate T1's concrete deliverable: a 'Theory Vocabulary Constitution' answering six fixed questions (what it is, what it is not, inputs, outputs, epistemic status, corpus-derived-or-proposed) for every core concept, with new primitives explicitly forbidden until this constitution is complete.

b_rows_sample.anchor: Step 2 -- Close K_t. What conditions make K in K-blackboard? Establish, rather than assume: identity, temporal status, provenance/history, propositions, evidence relations, uncertainty, context, inquiry, status, revision state. The historical 10-component decomposition should not automatically become the canonical ontology. Which properties are mathematically necessary for a Knowledge State, independent of one particular representation? That distinction prevents the V7/Sigma problem from happening again.
b_rows_sample.statement: Proposes Gate T2's core research question (what conditions make K admissible in K-blackboard) and explicitly generalizes the V7/Sigma lesson from this same day's F4 audit into a standing methodological rule: the historical 10-component K_t decomposition must not automatically become canonical ontology, to prevent repeating that exact failure mode.

b_rows_sample.anchor: Step 3 -- Close Proposition Semantics. Represent -> Interpret -> Support -> Determine -> Revise/Refute. Formal answers needed for: proposition identity, proposition version, negation, conjunction/disjunction, quantification, temporal propositions, conflicting propositions, unknown propositions. Prerequisite to rigorous evidence and satisfaction semantics.
b_rows_sample.statement: Proposes Gate T3's complete proposition lifecycle (Represent->Interpret->Support->Determine->Revise/Refute) and eight required formal sub-answers (identity, version, negation, conjunction/disjunction, quantification, temporal, conflicting, unknown propositions) as prerequisite to evidence/satisfaction semantics.

b_rows_sample.anchor: Step 4 -- Close Evidence Semantics. Evidence -> Support/Challenge -> Warrant -> Determination. But do not collapse these. Formal distinction needed between Supported(p) and True(p). If you eventually want Supported(p) => True(p), that requires a separately justified soundness bridge. Otherwise the implication is invalid.
b_rows_sample.statement: Requires a formal separation of Supported(p) from True(p), explicitly conditioning any future Supported(p)=>True(p) implication on a separately justified soundness bridge, forbidding the implication otherwise.

b_rows_sample.anchor: Step 5 -- Sat(K_t,r), the major remaining problem: this is where your current F4 research lands. What does it mean for K_t to satisfy r? You should not immediately define Sat(K_t,r)=[pi_i(K_t) in Accept_r]. That was precisely the danger exposed by MD-061. Instead investigate r -> ? <- K_t and determine what corpus evidence establishes the relation. Recover: 1. What exactly is r? 2. What makes r a requirement? 3. What is its acceptance criterion? 4. What information in K_t is relevant? 5. What constitutes satisfaction? 6. Can satisfaction be partial? 7. Can it be unknown? 8. Can it be conflicted? 9. Is satisfaction binary or graded? 10. Can satisfaction be independently validated? Only after that can Sat be frozen.
b_rows_sample.statement: Explicitly names Gate T5 (Sat(K_t,r)) as the field's major remaining problem and where the day's F4 research lands, forbids repeating MD-061's premature component-membership definition, and lists ten explicit recovery questions that must be answered before Sat can be frozen.

b_rows_sample.anchor: Step 6 -- close the Knowledge Gap. Zero(K_t,R_t) iff Delta_t=empty. Monotonicity: K_t<=K_{t+1} =?=> Delta_{t+1} subseteq Delta_t. This may not be universally true because new knowledge can reveal new requirements. So you must test it rather than assume it. Revision: can Delta_t=empty become Delta_{t+1}!=empty? Yes, potentially, if requirements change or previous satisfaction is retracted. That makes Zero a state-relative condition, not necessarily an irreversible terminal state.
b_rows_sample.statement: Proposes two testable (not assumed) properties for Delta_t/Zero once Sat is established: a monotonicity conjecture (more knowledge implies a smaller or equal gap, explicitly flagged as possibly false since new knowledge can reveal new requirements) and a revision property (an empty gap can become non-empty again if requirements change or prior satisfaction is retracted), concluding Zero is state-relative, not necessarily an irreversible terminal state.

b_rows_sample.anchor: Step 7 -- close Transformation Theory. Q_q(T(K))=Q_q(K) for the relevant domain. This gives a rigorous basis for reduction, elimination, abstraction, compression, projection, normalization, representation change. A transformation is valid relative to what the inquiry requires it to preserve. That is much safer than claiming that transformations preserve 'meaning' in some absolute sense.
b_rows_sample.statement: States the inquiry-preservation criterion Q_q(T(K))=Q_q(K) as the rigorous basis for the whole reduction/elimination/abstraction/compression/projection/normalization family, explicitly favoring inquiry-relative validity over any claim of absolute meaning preservation.

b_rows_sample.anchor: Step 8 -- solve semantic equivalence. r1 ~_q r2 iff Q_q(r1(K))=Q_q(r2(K)) over an admissible domain. Instead of saying 'F3 and F4 mean the same thing,' you ask: Do F3 and F4 preserve the same inquiry-relevant observables? That is a mathematically testable question.
b_rows_sample.statement: Proposes an inquiry-relative candidate definition for semantic equivalence (r1 ~_q r2 iff their Q_q observables match), explicitly reframing the F3<->F4 comparison problem from an untestable identity claim into a mathematically testable inquiry-preservation question.

b_rows_sample.anchor: Step 9 -- close Decision and Action. KnowledgeState -> Determination -> Decision -> Authorization -> Action. Do not collapse Determination=Decision. A determination may say P is supported. A decision may say Choose A. Authorization may say Actor x may execute A. Action then changes the world W_t ->[A]-> W_{t+1}. That produces new observations and therefore new evidence: W_{t+1} -> O_{t+1} -> E_{t+1} -> K_{t+1}. This closes the epistemic feedback loop.
b_rows_sample.statement: States Gate T9's required five-stage chain (KnowledgeState->Determination->Decision->Authorization->Action) with explicit prohibition against collapsing Determination and Decision, and closes the epistemic feedback loop by tracing Action back through new World state, Observation, Evidence, into K_{t+1}.

b_rows_sample.anchor: The actual order I recommend: T1 Vocabulary/boundaries -> T2 Knowledge State K_t -> T3 Proposition -> T4 Evidence+Warrant -> T5 Requirement+Sat(K,r) -> T6 Gap Delta+Zero -> T7 Transformation+Preservation -> T8 Semantic Equivalence -> T9 Determination->Decision->Authorization->Action -> T10 F3<->F4 semantic comparison -> T11 Operation minimality -> T12 Architecture/implementation. Do not work on operation minimality yet. You currently have competing descriptions of required capabilities, but no justified canonical minimal operation basis. Theory -> Capability requirements -> Operation candidates must remain separate from Canonical minimal operation set. The latter should come much later.
b_rows_sample.statement: Extends the nine theory gates into a twelve-item ordered research programme (T1-T12, ending in architecture/implementation), with an explicit correction from an earlier roadmap: operation minimality (T11) must be deferred until theory closure, since capability requirements and operation candidates must remain separate from any canonical minimal operation set.

b_rows_sample.anchor: If the goal is to finish KnowledgeOS Theory rather than merely write more theory, the next concrete research mission should be: T5 -- Formal closure audit of Requirement and Satisfaction Semantics. r -> R_t -> Sat(K_t,r) -> Delta_t -> Zero. For every arrow, determine: DERIVED/RECONSTRUCTABLE/ASSUMED/HYPOTHESIS/NOT ESTABLISHED/RESEARCH REQUIRED. That single audit will tell us whether the current theory can genuinely proceed to computable Knowledge Gap and Zero, or whether another semantic foundation is still missing. Are we recovering KnowledgeOS theory from the corpus, or designing theory because the corpus is incomplete? We should answer that component by component, rather than giving one global answer.
b_rows_sample.statement: Recommends T5 (a formal closure audit of the five-arrow chain r->R_t->Sat(K_t,r)->Delta_t->Zero, each arrow classified via a six-value vocabulary DERIVED/RECONSTRUCTABLE/ASSUMED/HYPOTHESIS/NOT-ESTABLISHED/RESEARCH-REQUIRED) as the single next concrete research mission, explicitly resolving the recovering-vs-designing question component by component rather than as one global verdict.

b_rows_sample.anchor: EPISTEMIC LABELS: Every claim must be classified as: DERIVED, RECONSTRUCTABLE, ASSUMED, HYPOTHESIS, NOT ESTABLISHED, RESEARCH REQUIRED.
b_rows_sample.statement: Mandates a six-value epistemic-label vocabulary (DERIVED/RECONSTRUCTABLE/ASSUMED/HYPOTHESIS/NOT-ESTABLISHED/RESEARCH-REQUIRED) for classifying every claim made during the audit, matching the six-value vocabulary recommended in this same batch's theory-closure-roadmap (S2900).

a_rows_sample.statement: The derived canonical Policy type: Policy=(id, version, Gates, ValidityInterval, ResolutionBehavior), where Gates is a set of three-valued predicates over a Decision, ValidityInterval is a half-open temporal window, and ResolutionBehavior maps Unknown to Block or Allow; the Apply function is a strict three-valued conjunction over Gates (False if any gate is False, ResolutionBehavior(Unknown) if any gate is Unknown and none is False, True otherwise, with no averaging), and Applicable(p,t) checks temporal membership in the validity interval — this directly answers gap G-2.
